Taj Mahal.history: Built between 1631 and 1653 by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan as a mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, the Taj Mahal is widely regarded as the finest example of Mughal architecture and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Taj Mahal.fun_fact: The minarets of the Taj Mahal lean slightly outward so they would fall away from the tomb in the event of an earthquake.

Humayun's Tomb.history: Completed in 1572, Humayun's Tomb was commissioned by Hamida Banu Begum and became the first great garden-tomb of the subcontinent, influencing later Mughal monuments including the Taj Mahal.
Humayun's Tomb.fun_fact: More than 150 members of the Mughal royal family are buried within the larger Humayun's Tomb complex.

Red Fort.history: The Red Fort was built between 1638 and 1648 by Shah Jahan when he shifted the Mughal capital from Agra to Shahjahanabad. Its red sandstone walls enclose palaces, ceremonial halls, and gardens.
Red Fort.fun_fact: India's Prime Minister hoists the national flag from the Red Fort every Independence Day.

Agra Fort.history: Agra Fort became the principal Mughal residence before the capital shifted to Delhi. Begun by Akbar in 1565, it was later expanded with marble palaces by Jahangir and Shah Jahan.
Agra Fort.built_by: Akbar (original), expanded by Jahangir and Shah Jahan
Agra Fort.fun_fact: Shah Jahan spent his last years imprisoned in Agra Fort with a distant view of the Taj Mahal.

Fatehpur Sikri.history: Fatehpur Sikri was built by Akbar in the 1570s as an imperial capital. Though occupied for only a short time, it remains one of the most complete surviving Mughal city complexes.
Fatehpur Sikri.fun_fact: The city is often described as a ghost capital because it was abandoned not long after completion.

Itmad-ud-Daulah.history: Often called the Baby Taj, Itmad-ud-Daulah was built between 1622 and 1628 by Nur Jahan for her father Mirza Ghiyas Beg. It is notable for its full marble surface and intricate pietra dura work.
Itmad-ud-Daulah.fun_fact: This monument helped popularize the marble inlay technique later perfected at the Taj Mahal.

Jama Masjid Delhi.history: Built by Shah Jahan between 1644 and 1656, the Jama Masjid is one of the largest and most important Mughal mosques in India, known for its broad courtyard and prominent domes.
Jama Masjid Delhi.fun_fact: The mosque was built by thousands of workers over roughly twelve years.

Qutub Minar.history: Qutub Minar predates the Mughals but remained part of the Indo-Islamic architectural heritage referenced and preserved in later periods. It is the world's tallest brick minaret.
Qutub Minar.built_by: Qutb ud-Din Aibak (founded), later completed and restored
Qutub Minar.fun_fact: Its tapering shaft is divided by projecting balconies that create a very distinctive silhouette.

Bibi Ka Maqbara.history: Built between 1651 and 1661 in memory of Dilras Banu Begum, Bibi Ka Maqbara is often called the Taj of the Deccan because of its strong visual resemblance to the Taj Mahal.
Bibi Ka Maqbara.fun_fact: Despite its resemblance to the Taj Mahal, it was built on a more limited budget with simpler materials and detailing.

Akbar's Tomb.history: Akbar's Tomb at Sikandra was begun by Akbar himself and completed by Jahangir in 1613. The monument is notable for combining multiple architectural influences within a distinctly Mughal plan.
Akbar's Tomb.fun_fact: Akbar is said to have taken an active interest in the early planning of his own mausoleum.

Buland Darwaza.history: Buland Darwaza was commissioned by Akbar around 1601 to celebrate his victory over Gujarat. It forms the dramatic southern gateway to the Jama Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri.
Buland Darwaza.fun_fact: Its monumental staircase greatly amplifies the visual height and theatrical impact of the gateway.

Tomb of Salim Chishti.history: The Tomb of Salim Chishti is a white marble shrine within the Jama Masjid complex at Fatehpur Sikri. It honors the Sufi saint Sheikh Salim Chishti, closely associated with Akbar's court.
Tomb of Salim Chishti.fun_fact: Visitors often tie threads to the marble lattice screens while making wishes at the shrine.

Shalimar Bagh.history: Shalimar Bagh was laid out by Jahangir in 1619 on the shores of Dal Lake and remains one of the finest surviving Mughal pleasure gardens in Kashmir.
Shalimar Bagh.fun_fact: Its terraces, channels, and fountains are designed to evoke the idea of a paradise garden.

Moti Masjid Agra.history: The Pearl Mosque inside Agra Fort was built by Shah Jahan between 1647 and 1654 for royal use. It is admired for its luminous white marble and restrained elegance.
Moti Masjid Agra.opening_hours: Part of Agra Fort timings (6:00 AM - 6:00 PM)
Moti Masjid Agra.fun_fact: The mosque is called the Pearl Mosque because its polished marble surface appears to glow softly like a pearl.

Safdarjung Tomb.history: Built in 1754 for Safdarjung, this monument is often regarded as the last great garden tomb of the Mughal tradition in India.
Safdarjung Tomb.fun_fact: Safdarjung's Tomb is frequently described as a late echo of the grand Mughal garden-tomb tradition.
